title: I Survived 100 Days as a Polar Bear Waiting for the Ice
description: Animal Secrets #25 — What if you were a young polar bear stuck on land for 100 days, waiting for Hudson Bay to freeze? A survival story, but every number is real: from collar-camera studies to the 180-day starvation line. Polar Bear Week 2026 just put hundreds of these bears on live cams in Churchill.
tags: i survived 100 days as a polar bear
polar bear survival day 1 to day 100
what if you were a polar bear

scenes.say: You hear that? The ice is cracking under my paws, and I haven't eaten in ninety-three days.
I'm a polar bear. I weigh way less than I should. And if this ice gives way, I go into freezing black water.
Okay, so this is a story. A what if. But every number you'll hear in it is real, from real scientists.
And by the end, you'll find out if I made it to Day 100. Let me take you back. Day 1.

scenes.label: Western Hudson Bay
scenes.say: Day 1. The last piece of sea ice I'm standing on is melting into slush.
Here's the thing. I'm a four-year-old female, about two hundred kilos. Out here on the ice is where I hunt.
Seals. Ringed seals, fifty to sixty-five kilos each, full of thick blubber. That fat is basically my whole year's fuel.
But every summer, Hudson Bay melts completely. No ice, no seals I can catch. So I have to swim to land.

scenes.label: 5x the energy
scenes.say: And swimming is expensive for me. At the same speed, it burns about five times more energy than walking.
I drag myself onto the shore, soaking wet. From today, I'm on a fast. No real food until the ice comes back.
How long is that? Nobody knows. That's the scary part.
Day 4. Wapusk National Park, Manitoba. Flat tundra, ponds, willows, and other bears doing exactly what I'm doing.
Nothing. We're all doing nothing. Because every step costs fat, and fat is the only thing keeping me alive.

scenes.label: -1 kg per day
scenes.say: Scientists say a fasting polar bear here loses around one kilo of body weight every single day.
Think about that. Every sunrise, a kilo of me just disappears.
Day 9. New danger, and it's tiny. Mosquitoes. Clouds of them, buzzing around my nose and eyes.
I'm built for Arctic winter. Summer on land feels like wearing a fur coat in a sauna.
I swat at them with a paw the size of a dinner plate. Missed. Every. Single. One. And swatting burns fuel too.
So I do what older bears do. I dig a cool day bed in the dirt and press my belly into it.
When the wind gets bad, I shove my head into a willow bush. Just my round rump sticking out. Not my best look.
Day 15. I smell something sweet. Berries! Little blue berries all over the tundra.
I eat for hours. My muzzle turns purple. For the first time in two weeks, I feel kind of full.
But here's the twist. Scientists put video collars on twenty bears here, and watched exactly what they ate.

scenes.label: 19 of 20 lost weight
scenes.say: Bears ate grass, kelp, berries, bird carcasses, even old caribou antlers. And nineteen of the twenty still lost weight.
Walking around to find berries burns almost everything the berries give you. I'm not a grizzly in a white coat.
So I stop wasting energy on snacks. And that's when the first real problem shows up.
Day 21. A giant male walks over the ridge. Huge. Maybe twice my weight.

scenes.label: 583 kg male
scenes.say: Adult males here can top five hundred kilos. In one study, the biggest weighed five hundred eighty-three.
He stops. He sniffs the air. My heart is pounding, but I don't run. Running burns way too much fuel.
I turn slowly, put my head down, and walk away, step by step. He doesn't follow. Today, he's too tired too.
Funny thing. That giant male in the study burned twenty-two thousand calories a day, because he never stopped moving.
The laziest male burned only four thousand three hundred. Lazy is how you survive out here.
Day 28. I'm starving, and I do something risky. I walk back into the water and start swimming.

scenes.label: Smell: 1 km+
scenes.say: Why? Because I can smell something out there. Polar bears can smell seals from more than a kilometer away.
I swim for hours. Paddling with my big front paws, back legs steering like a rudder.
And then I see it. A dead beluga whale, floating. A mountain of fat. Exactly what I need.
But I can't eat it. Not in the water. I try and try, and I just slip off.

scenes.label: 175 km swim
scenes.say: This really happened. A young female in that study swam one hundred seventy-five kilometers and found a beluga carcass.
Over six hours, she was seen eating for only thirty-five seconds. She mostly used it as a floating pillow.
So I do the same. I rest my chin on it, catch my breath, and let it go. Then the long swim back.
Day 34. I crawl back onto land, more tired than ever. I've lost maybe thirty-something kilos already.
And the bad news is, the calendar is not on my side.

scenes.label: +3 to 4 weeks
scenes.say: Scientists say the ice-free season here is now three to four weeks longer than in the early 1980s.
That's a whole extra month my grandmother never had to go without food. Hudson Bay warmed over one degree in thirty years.
And there's a number that haunts every bear on this coast. About one hundred eighty days.

scenes.label: 63% of young bears
scenes.say: That's roughly the limit. Fast that long, and up to sixty-three percent of young bears like me could starve.
Okay. I'm on Day 34. Deep breath. Keep going.
Day 42. A storm rolls in off the bay. Wind, rain, then the first wet snow of the season.
Snow sounds good, right? Cold means ice. But it's way too early. The bay is still wide open water.
I curl into a ball in my day bed. Fur, fat, and a black nose tucked into my paws.
When the storm clears, a little white face is watching me. An Arctic fox.
Foxes follow polar bears out onto the ice, hoping for leftovers. This one is going to be very disappointed. I have nothing.
We stare at each other for a long time. Then it trots off. Smart fox. It knows a hungry bear when it sees one.

scenes.label: Halfway: about -50 kg
scenes.say: Day 50. Halfway. If I lose about a kilo a day, I've lost around fifty kilos since Day 1.
My hips are sticking out. My coat looks too big for me.
But here's what keeps me going. All along this coast, hundreds of other bears are doing exactly this too. I'm not alone.
Subscribe if you're still with me. We've got fifty more days, and they get way harder.
Day 57. My nose wakes me up at sunrise. Something big and dead washed up on the beach.

scenes.label: +32 kg jackpot
scenes.say: A seal carcass. On land. This is the jackpot. One bear in that study found something like this, and gained thirty-two kilos.
I run. Well, I trot. Polar bears can hit around twenty-five miles an hour, but I don't have that kind of energy now.
And of course, the giant male from Day 21 is already there. Eating. Huge chunks of blubber.
A polar bear can eat about forty-five kilos in one sitting. He's not sharing.
So I try the polite way. I lie low, circle slowly, and reach my nose toward his. That's how bears ask nicely.
He growls. I back off. But when he finally walks away, he leaves scraps. Not a feast. But it's something.
Day 64. Fall is coming, and I start drifting north along the coast. Toward a town called Churchill.
Every autumn, hundreds of us gather near this town, waiting for the bay to freeze first along the shore.
And this town smells amazing. Garbage, cooking, warm buildings. For a starving bear, it's pure temptation.
Then a strange buzzing thing flies over my head. A drone. People here test them to scare bears away without hurting us.
They even have smart cameras that warn people when a bear is close. Like a doorbell camera that says, polar bear outside.
Good. Towns are where bears get into trouble. I turn around and head back to the tundra.
Walking away from food when you're this hungry? That might be the hardest thing I've done all summer.
Day 71. Something new. A mother bear with two cubs walks by. Wait. One of those cubs looks different.

scenes.label: 13 adoptions
scenes.say: This is real too. Mothers here have adopted cubs that weren't theirs. Scientists have recorded thirteen cases.
One was caught on camera as recently as fall twenty twenty-five. Out here, sometimes even a bear gets a second family.

scenes.label: 8 months, no meals
scenes.say: And moms have it even harder than me. A pregnant female here can go about eight months between meals.
So if you think I'm hungry, imagine her.
Day 78. On the shore, two huge males stand up on their back legs and start wrestling.
But it's not a real fight. It's called sparring. Practice. It keeps their hunting muscles strong while they wait.
That night, the sky turns green. The northern lights. Churchill sits right under them.
For a moment, I forget I'm hungry. Then my stomach growls louder than that male bear did.
Day 85. Real cold, finally. The snow geese are gone south. The ponds are frozen solid.
And along the shore, the sea looks different. Thick and oily. Grease ice. The bay is starting to freeze.
Every bear on the coast is lined up at the edge, staring at the water. Waiting.
Some bears test it with one paw, like you test a cold pool with your toe. Then they pull back. Smart.
But this is the most dangerous part. That ice is way too thin to hold me. Not yet.
Day 93. The grease ice has turned into round plates. Pancake ice, bumping into each other.
I can smell seals out there. The hunger is louder than my common sense. I step on.
And this is where you came in. The ice is cracking under my paws.
I spread my legs wide, flatten my belly, and slide. Spreading my weight like a giant furry snowshoe.
Crack. My back leg plunges into black water. Ice cold. I'm thrashing, but I can't climb out.
Then I remember. Don't fight the ice. Swim to the shore side, where it's thicker, and push up with my front paws.
I haul out. Shaking. Soaked. Alive. And I make a promise. I'll wait a few more days. Patience is a polar bear's real superpower.
Day 97. A massive blizzard hits. Howling wind, freezing cold. And for once, that's the best news ever.
Because cold wind is exactly what freezes Hudson Bay. All night, I can hear the ice growing, creaking and groaning.
I'm at my lightest. I'm guessing a hundred kilos lighter than Day 1. But the finish line is right there.
Day 100. Morning. The bay is white all the way to the horizon. Solid, real sea ice. No more slush.
I step on. It holds. I step again. It holds. I'm walking on the ocean again.
Far out, I find a little breathing hole a ringed seal keeps open in the ice. And I wait. Totally still.

scenes.label: Under 2% succeed
scenes.say: Most hunts fail. Sometimes less than two percent work. So I wait, and wait.
Then, a soft splash under the ice. I won't show the rest. Let's just say, I finally eat.
My first meal in one hundred days. And the ice will feed me until summer comes again.
And guess who shows up for the leftovers? My little fox friend from Day 42. Fine. You earned it, buddy.

scenes.label: -30% since 1987
scenes.say: But here's what bugs me. Bears in this part of the bay have declined by about thirty percent since 1987.
And every extra day without ice is one more kilo they have to lose. That's the real story behind this one.
The lesson? Sometimes surviving isn't about being the strongest. It's about not wasting a single bit of energy.
Now tell me in the comments. Would you rather survive 100 days as a polar bear, or as a fox following one?

short.title: This Polar Bear Hasn't Eaten in 93 Days
short.description: Hudson Bay polar bears fast on land until the ice comes back, losing about 1 kg a day. Full Day 1 to Day 100 story on the channel.

scenes.say: You hear that? The ice is cracking under me, and I haven't eaten in ninety-three days.
I'm a polar bear on Hudson Bay. Every summer the ice melts, and I'm stuck on land with no seals to hunt.
Scientists say bears like me lose about one kilo a day while we wait. Every single day.
And the wait is now three to four weeks longer than it was in the early 1980s.
So when the first thin ice forms, I smell seals out there and I step on. Too early. My leg breaks through into black water. Can I climb out before the cold wins?
Full story on my channel. But first, do you hear that?
